questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere where they spoke English and where I would feel like I could challenge myself socially and academically and experience a new part of the world.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My stay in Seattle was an amazing experience for me. It is a very easy city to like and has a very European vibe to it. The people are so kind and helpful and there is plenty of amazing things to do both in the city and in the nature around the city. UW is a really good university and I was very overwhelmed by the academic and personal engagement from my peers and professors.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very hard. The Danish system for going abroad overseas is complicated to understand and the other Danes going to Seattle and I were constantly met with either lack of help or differing responses to the same question. The host institution however was very helpful at all hours and gave more than sufficient information upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: FIUTS the international student organization, sent me many emails and a woman named Sarah Berryman was a significant help whenever something was confusing or challenging.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It's hard but you will succeed eventually. I strongly recommend not staying on campus. The ones that live there are very young (teenagers) and the dorms are very bad quality.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's a great way to make American friends. It is also expensive. I recommend looking for housing in either U-district or in that area around U-district. I lived in Wedgwood and that worked well with a short bus ride or a bike ride to school.  I recommend going on facebook and finding groups for housing in Seattle or going on craigslist, that's where I found my roommates.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's a bit tricky to understand the registration process in the first round of registration, but there is no need to worry. Even if classes are filled they often still take you in.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You add classes on their "my plan" page and then you attend them for the first week and maybe drop or change a class if it's not for you.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A lot a the international student's service office. Again, Sarah Berryman was my hero.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. I got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Think twice about taking graduate courses. It is a great way to learn, but watch the workload, cause it's basically PHD classes, so maybe mix graduate and undergrad classes and prioritize one class more than the other.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The workload is higher but the expectations for your work are not the same as at KU. They do not expect you to break your neck like a 72-hour exam at KU. The level is a bit lower all depending on the class you choose. Graduate was hard and very high level, but Undergrad was easy but with more papers.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It's way more engaging and fun. The professors care a lot about creating a talkative and discussion-based learning environment. I felt like I learned a lot more this way than at KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: In the first quarter I had African American Political Theory, African American Politics: How Does it Feel to Be a Problem? and Ethnic Politics  in the US and Beyond. In the second I had Middle East in the Modern World and Social Reproductive Theory

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I strongly recommend taking classes with Oliver Rollins, Jonathan Warren, and Jey Saung. Both are amazing teachers of critical race theory and feminist theory. In general, they are experts on anti-capitalist works and anti-colonialism. UW has some amazing classes on critical theory that KU would never even consider having, so diving into that was an incredible learning experience.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Doctor's bills. Even though you are ensured it still costs money to go to the doctor.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
UW provides a Husky Card which gives you free rides on all public transport in Seattle. So that was nice. 
Food is so so expensive though. It's delicious but expensive. Particularly groceries.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have an amazing gym with literally everything from climbing centers to tennis courts to masseuses.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a club for everything, all kinds of sports clubs, movie clubs, heritage clubs, hiking clubs etc. etc. FIUTS did a lot of social events.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking, kayaking, concerts, eating Asian food and fish, the cinema, and bouldering. Also biking the Burke Gilman Trail.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go on a trip to the mountains. It is so beautiful out in nature. 
I also went to Portland and Vancouver BC (both 4 hours bus ride away), which was a lot of fun.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Americans (and Pacific North Westeners) are very easy-going and kind to you.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Ask them out for coffee. You have to push yourself a lot to do those things where you just ask people out in the first while and then suddenly you have great friends. 
If you find it hard to find friends at uni, you can also use Bumble Friends to find friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really any. Seattle people are very easy people.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and kindness Americans show to strangers like yourself.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to be vulnerable in terms of approaching new people, remember to get out into nature, and remember that once you return you will have forgotten your grades from class but the time you spent exploring.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Apply for scholarships. It's an expensive time.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting and getting to know my American friends, experiencing nature and academic learnings.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being so far away from home with such a big time difference.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
